tutorial.title: Creating Variables
tutorial.descriptionContent: Learn how to create variables in JavaScript.

lessons.title: JavaScript
lessons.interactiveContent:
Welcome to JavaScript, a versatile coding language.

We'll take an in depth look into Javascript, a programming language that powers dynamic websites and apps.

lessons.title: Moving boxes
lessons.interactiveContent:
Dynamic websites need to remember information to display or change. For that, JavaScript has variables.

Like moving boxes, variables have content and names that tell us what's inside.

lessons.title: Writing let and const
lessons.interactiveContent:
We use let, and const to create variables. We'll use both for now and cover the difference between them later.

Make sure to pick const.

lessons.title: Creating a name with no spaces
lessons.interactiveContent:
Every variable needs a name. Variable names need to be single words and, therefore, have no spaces.

Make sure to pick city.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Every variable needs a name with no spaces. Use let to begin a variable named city.

Make sure to pick let, followed by city.

lessons.title: Using camel case
lessons.interactiveContent:
To create variable names with multiple words, we use camel case. We start with a lowercase letter and capitalize the additional words.

Make sure to pick homeCity.
lessons.hardModeContent:
For multiple-word variable names, use camel case: start lowercase and capitalize added words. Name the home city.

Make sure to pick homeCity.

lessons.title: Giving a name
lessons.interactiveContent:
To help us understand what's inside a variable we pick descriptive names.

Make sure to pick windyCity.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You pick descriptive names to show what a variable will store. Combine windy and city using camel case.

Make sure to pick windyCity.

It contains a space.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Look at the declaration. Why cannot JavaScript use this as one variable name?

The name contains a space, so JavaScript reads two separate words.The capital letter makes the name invalid.Variable names must begin with a capital letter.

The name contains a space, so JavaScript reads two separate words.

lessons.title: Question 2

lessons.hardModeContent:
A teammate sees const country = "Japan". Why is country better than x?

It communicates what value the variable contains.It makes the program run faster.JavaScript does not allow one-letter variable names.

It communicates what value the variable contains.

lessons.title: Using numbers
lessons.interactiveContent:
Variable names can contain numbers, too. Adding numbers is useful with multiple similar variables. Let's create the variable car1 here.

Make sure to pick car1.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Variable names can contain numbers to distinguish similar variables. Use 1 in a name for the first car.

Make sure to pick car1.

lessons.title: Giving a variable a value
lessons.interactiveContent:
After creating and naming a variable, we use the = sign to store a value inside it. Like const city = "Chicago".

Make sure to pick =, followed by "Chicago".
lessons.hardModeContent:
After naming a variable, use = to store a value. Store "Chicago" in city.

Make sure to pick city, followed by =, and finally "Chicago".

lessons.title: Completing your first variable
lessons.interactiveContent:
To finish creating a variable, we put a semicolon, ;, at the end of the line.

Make sure to pick ;.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You finish creating a variable with a semicolon, ;. Store "Chicago" in city and end the line.

Make sure to pick city, followed by =, "Chicago", and finally ;.

lessons.title: String
lessons.interactiveContent:
The values we've been storing like "Chicago" are strings. Strings are words in double quotes.

Make sure to pick ", followed by ".
lessons.hardModeContent:
Values like "Chicago" are strings. Use double quotes to write Chicago as a string.

Make sure to pick ", followed by Chicago, and finally ".

lessons.title: Sentence
lessons.interactiveContent:
Strings can contain all sorts of letters and symbols, including spaces. For example, "Winter is coming.".

Make sure to pick ", followed by Winter is coming., and finally ".
lessons.hardModeContent:
Strings can contain letters, symbols, and spaces. Use double quotes to create "Winter is coming.".

Make sure to pick ", followed by Winter is coming., and finally ".

lessons.title: Intro
lessons.interactiveContent: We already know we can declare variables with let and const. Let's find out the difference between them!

lessons.title: Const
lessons.interactiveContent:
We use const to declare variables whose values are not supposed to change. const is short for "constant".

Make sure to pick const, followed by norwayCapital.
lessons.hardModeContent:
We use const to declare variables whose values are not supposed to change. const is short for "constant".

Store "Oslo" in the unchanged norwayCapital variable.

Make sure to pick const, followed by norwayCapital, and finally =.

lessons.title: const update
lessons.interactiveContent: If we try to update a value stored in a const variable, we will get an error.

lessons.title: Let vs const update
lessons.interactiveContent:
However, we can update let variables with the assign = operator.

Make sure to pick let.
lessons.hardModeContent:
However, we can update let variables with the assign = operator.

Choose the keyword that allows age to later become 91.

Make sure to pick let, followed by =.

lessons.title: CONST
lessons.interactiveContent:
To make it obvious that a variable is of type const and shouldn't change, we can optionally name it with uppercase letters.

Create an uppercase birthday constant.

Make sure to pick BIRTHDAY.
lessons.hardModeContent:
The keyword const is short for constant. Its variable cannot be reassigned.

You can optionally use uppercase letters to show a constant. Declare it with the uppercase name BIRTHDAY.

Make sure to pick const, followed by BIRTHDAY.

lessons.title: CONST_SNAKE_CASE
lessons.interactiveContent:
We cannot use camelCase if we use this uppercase standard, so we use an uppercase snake_case to name variables with more than one word.

Create an uppercase "speed of light" const using snake_case.

Make sure to pick SPEED_OF_LIGHT.
lessons.hardModeContent:
We cannot use camelCase if we use this uppercase standard, so we use an uppercase snake_case to name variables with more than one word.

Store "3*10⁸ m/s" in the uppercase speed-of-light constant.

Make sure to pick const, followed by SPEED_OF_LIGHT, and finally =.

lessons.title: Default const
lessons.interactiveContent:
Both let and const are useful variables and we could use them interchangeably. However, we should try to use const as default.

Make sure to pick const.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You should use const by default. Use let when you need to assign a new value later.

Declare the constant MIDDLE_NAME with the value "Francesca".

Make sure to pick const, followed by MIDDLE_NAME.

truefalse

lessons.hardModeContent:

Yes, because let variables can be updated.No, because let values are fixed.No, because only const can be reassigned.

Yes, because let variables can be updated.

lessons.title: Lines of code
lessons.interactiveContent:
Lines of code are instructions for the computer to follow.

When we run code, we tell the computer to follow the instructions we put together.

lessons.title: Order
lessons.interactiveContent:
The order of the instructions matters because the computer follows the instructions line by line.

Create step1 first, step2 second, and step3 third.

Make sure to pick const step1 = "Collect pants";, followed by const step2 = "?";, and finally const step3 = "Profit";.
lessons.hardModeContent:
The order matters because the computer follows instructions line by line.

Create step1 with "Collect pants", then step2 with "?", then step3 with "Profit".

Make sure to pick const step1 = "Collect pants";, followed by const step2 = "?";, and finally const step3 = "Profit";.

lessons.title: Console
lessons.interactiveContent:
With the special instruction console.log(), we tell the computer to display a value in an area called the console.

Make sure to pick "Hello, World!".
lessons.hardModeContent:
With the special instruction console.log(), we tell the computer to display a value in an area called the console.

Display "Hello, World!" in the console.

Make sure to pick console.log, followed by "Hello, World!".

lessons.title: Displaying multiple times
lessons.interactiveContent:
We can use the console.log() instruction as often as we want. The computer displays every value on a line in the console.

Make sure to pick (, followed by ).
lessons.hardModeContent:
We can use the console.log() instruction as often as we want. The computer displays every value on a line in the console.

Make the countdown display "3, 2, 1" and then "GO!".

Make sure to pick console.log, followed by console.log, and finally "GO!".

lessons.title: Displaying variables
lessons.interactiveContent:
We can use console.log() to display variables like greeting, too.

Make sure to pick greeting.
lessons.hardModeContent:
We can use console.log() to display variables like greeting, too.

Pass the variable greeting to the call to display its stored value.

Make sure to pick console.log, followed by greeting.

lessons.title: Output
lessons.interactiveContent:
When we display variables in the console, their values appear instead of their names. If we log name here, it'll show its value.

Make sure to pick name.
lessons.hardModeContent:
When we display variables in the console, their values appear instead of their names. If we log name here, it will show its value.

Pass the variable name to the call so the console displays Daenerys.

Make sure to pick console.log, followed by name.
